questions.q: Why is ensembling especially valuable in quantitative finance, beyond general ML practice?
options: Because it guarantees a higher R² no matter what
Because financial signal is so faint that diversifying away each model's idiosyncratic error is often a bigger win than finding a single marginally better model
Because it eliminates the need for any validation
Because it only works with neural networks
questions.explain: With signal this faint, canceling out each model's distinct mistakes by combining models with different biases is often more valuable than searching for one 'best' model.

questions.q: What is the core idea behind combining models like Ridge, a random forest, and a boosted tree?
options: Using only the single best-performing model and discarding the rest
Each model makes different mistakes due to different biases, so averaging their predictions cancels idiosyncratic error while preserving shared real signal
Training all models on exactly the same architecture
Running each model with the same random seed to ensure identical outputs
questions.explain: This mirrors portfolio diversification: combining models whose errors are not perfectly correlated reduces overall error variance.

options: It trains a meta-model on out-of-fold predictions
It fits all specified base models and combines their predictions through a fixed (optionally weighted) average
It selects only one base model to use
It performs feature selection before training
questions.explain: VotingRegressor fits each base estimator and averages their outputs, with weights that can be set explicitly or left equal by default.

options: StackingRegressor uses no base models at all
StackingRegressor trains a meta-model on the base models' out-of-fold predictions to learn how to weight their contributions, rather than using a fixed average
StackingRegressor can only be used with linear models
StackingRegressor ignores the training data entirely
questions.explain: Instead of a fixed weighted average, StackingRegressor's final_estimator learns an optimal combination of base-model predictions from their out-of-fold outputs.

questions.q: What is the important caution about the `cv` parameter inside `StackingRegressor` when applied to real financial data?
options: It should always be set to cv=1
A plain K-fold split can leak information due to overlapping, non-IID financial labels -- a walk-forward or purged splitter should be used instead
The cv parameter has no effect in StackingRegressor
It must always match the number of base estimators
questions.explain: Because financial labels often overlap in time (Lesson 4), a naive K-fold inside StackingRegressor's internal cross-validation can leak information -- a walk-forward or purged splitter avoids this.
